records.abstract: Online discourse is dominated by a small portion of the world’s 7,000+ languages. CSA Research tracks the online use of languages and has identified approximately 130 with evidence of online communities with appreciable economic opportunity. Out of those 130 languages, speakers of 17 of them represent the overwhelming majority of online value and population – we refer to those languages as Tier One (“Top Online Languages (2024)”). By contrast, populations that speak “digitally disadvantaged” languages have little or no viable path to participation in the digital economy.

records.title: Investing in languages of india
records.subtitle: Guidance on the value and opportunity of india’s primary languages
records.display_title: Investing in languages of india: Guidance on the value and opportunity of india’s primary languages
records.abstract: With 22 “scheduled” (official) languages and English in wide use, India represents the most linguistically diverse major market in the world. Although most major global brands address India via English or, occasionally, Hindi, 14 language reach at least 10 million online consumers in the country. Hindi and English are effective vehicles for reaching audiences, but primarily as non-native languages. Adding additional languages can help improve customer experience in India and build deeper connections with populations. This report delivers figures for population and economic potential from both online and offline audiences for 22 languages in India. It then outlines four strategies involving progressively more in-depth localization to help brands reach audiences within India.

records.title: Where’s my translation jet pack?
records.display_title: Where’s my translation jet pack?
records.abstract:
Where’s My Translation Jet Pack? looks at decades of promises that technology would transform translation and asks why translators still spend so much of their time on repetitive and administrative work. Drawing on the history of machine translation and computer-assisted translation, the economics of language services, and emerging neural technologies, the presentation argues for a shift from automation centered on replacing human work to augmented translation: an interconnected environment in which adaptive MT, translation memory, terminology, content enrichment, and automated project management amplify human expertise. The talk anticipates a future in which machines absorb much of the industry's routine work while linguists remain at the center of multilingual communication.

In the time since I delivered this keynote, many of the trends I warned about have only accelerated and gone further toward marginalizing professional translators, but the promise of technology as an augmentation aid remains.
records.citation: November 2018. “Where’s my translation jetpack”. Keynote presentation at AsLing, Translating and the Computer 40, November 11, 2018.
